column3: It gives believers an active discipline of patience, steadfastness, vigilance, and God-consciousness aimed at success.
It makes success the outcome of weighty deeds, adding an accounting horizon to the focus's promised flourishing.
It specifies doing good as a communal practice of calling to good, enjoining right, and restraining wrong.
It joins God-consciousness, seeking the way to God, and striving with the same promised success.
Its nearby account of messengers chosen from angels and people supplies only the immediate revelatory setting.
The accusation against Abraham does not clarify worship, good action, or success in the focus.
It directly grounds worship of the Lord in His creation of people and those before them.
It provides a local negative outcome for those striving against the signs, but adds little to the focus's positive command.
It places bowing and prostration among the ordered devotions at the purified House.
It identifies usury as conduct to avoid while joining God-consciousness to the prospect of success.
It portrays believers as repeatedly bowing and prostrating while seeking God's favor, with righteous deeds also named.
Its claim that visible superiority is success supplies only a contrast to the focus's moral and devotional path.
It connects steadfastness and abundant remembrance in a crisis with the prospect of success.
As the preceding ayah, it frames the return of all affairs to God before the focus's imperative response.
It joins exclusive devotion, purification of the House, and its worshippers who stand, bow, and prostrate.
Its paired imperatives to prostrate and worship God closely restate the devotional center of the focus.
The nearby declaration of God's comprehensive knowledge provides a broad setting, not a distinct instruction.
Moses's past act and Pharaoh's accusation do not illuminate the focus's command sequence.
The refusal to bow when commanded gives a concise contrary response to the focus's command to bow.
The announcement of a clear Book adds no specific link to worship, good action, or success.
It marks fabricating lies about God or denying His signs as conduct that cannot succeed.
It directly commands devoted obedience, prostration, and bowing with those who bow.
The following ayah extends the focus into striving, prayer, almsgiving, and holding fast to God.
It contrasts true guidance and the lasting outcome with the failure of wrongdoers.
It directly exposes the gap between saying and doing, sharpening the focus's command to do good.
Its completion of vows and circling of the Ancient House extends the surah's concrete pilgrimage-devotion setting.
It carries glorification into the night and after prostrations, extending worship beyond the moment of bowing.
It links remembering God's favors with success, but its historical warning is less direct than earlier action commands.
It depicts servants of the Merciful spending the night in prostration and standing before their Lord.
It makes false attribution to God incompatible with success, a negative boundary for the focus's faithful address.
Love of worldly good does not clarify the commanded good action in the focus.
It makes sacrifice a divine rite joined to God's remembrance, gratitude, and feeding others in the same surah context.
It presents selfless preference for others over personal need as a social form of conduct joined to success.
The opening warning about the Hour offers a local eschatological frame but no direct account of the commands here.
Moses's helpful act and request for good supply only a distant narrative instance of beneficence.
It warns that possessions and children can divert believers from remembering God, yielding loss instead of flourishing.
It explicitly redirects prostration from the sun and moon to God their Creator.
Its condemnation of serving false powers does not add a distinct explanation after the clearer worship contrasts.
The question about the companions of the elephant does not clarify the focus's devotional and ethical sequence.
Withholding when good reaches a person does not materially develop the focus's command to do good.
Its believing response to recognized truth offers only a general example of faith's receptive posture.
It explicitly joins establishing prayer, giving alms, and bowing with those who bow.
The law of equitable retaliation and forgiveness supplies a broad ethical context but no close link to the focus.
Trust in God when others turn away is a general devotional response rather than a parallel to the command sequence.
It joins striving with wealth and selves, good things, and success, extending active faith beyond the focus's wording.
Its portrait of believers combines repentance, worship, praise, bowing, prostration, moral action, and faithfulness.
The warning to Moses to leave the city does not clarify worship, good action, or flourishing.
It names active fulfillment of almsgiving as a concrete deed within a successful believers' profile.
It couples worship of God alone with an extensive list of beneficent obligations to others.
It distinguishes the false objects of worship from their followers, providing a limited warning against misdirected devotion.
It commands God-consciousness, hearing, obedience, and spending for good, then links freedom from avarice to success.
Its instruction on hostile allegiances is an ethical command to believers but only indirectly related to the focus.
The specific command about fighting nearby disbelievers does not add to the focus's worship-and-good-action pattern.
It distinguishes the impure from the good and joins God-consciousness to success.
It portrays attachment to worldly good as distracting from remembrance of the Lord, a limited contrary example.
The oath by the clear Book does not develop the focus's commands.
It defines the successful as those whose scales are weighty, reinforcing the deeds-and-outcome connection.
The human desire for good and despair under harm do not explain worship or doing good here.
Divine acceptance after hardship supplies a distant example of mercy and return, not the focus's central sequence.
It again condemns saying what is not done, reinforcing the practical force of doing good after the earlier clearer parallel.
Knowledge of what people do adds a general accountability frame for the focus's commanded deeds.
The description of Hell adds no specific link to the focus.
It rejects calling on another god without proof and says such deniers do not succeed.
Witnessing persecution of believers does not clarify the focus's worship, beneficence, or success.
The angels' unanimous prostration supplies a distinct collective image of prostration, though its object differs from the focus.
Moses's acknowledgement of a past act does not add to the focus's instruction.
It identifies corrupt practices to shun and explicitly makes avoidance a path toward success.
The oath by the Quran of remembrance does not materially develop the focus.
It directly makes purification a condition of success, adding an inward discipline to the focus's actions.
It directs believers to seek help through patience and prayer, a practical support for sustained obedience.
The list of former confederate peoples does not clarify the focus.
It again denies success to wrongdoers while pointing to the final outcome, but repeats an earlier negative boundary.
It gives a concrete interpersonal ethic, calling proper entry and greeting good for believers.
The exchange among groups entering the Fire does not add to the focus's command pattern.
It directly depicts all in the heavens and earth prostrating to God, voluntarily or unwillingly.
It joins grateful use of wholesome provision with worship of God, extending devotion into ordinary provision.
It says sorcerers do not succeed, a narrow negative use of the same success vocabulary.
It sends believers from prayer into the earth to seek God's bounty while continuing remembrance, aimed at success.
The command for angels to prostrate before Adam is a distinct narrative prostration and adds little after stronger parallels.
The agricultural image and its marital instruction do not clarify the focus's good action or worship sequence.
The recording of all deeds provides only a general accountability setting.
Its instruction on a particular form of speech does not materially illuminate the focus.
It joins pilgrimage timing, proper conduct, God-consciousness, and the prospect of success.
It presents fasting as a prescribed discipline for believers aimed at God-consciousness.
Its glorification of the Lord in recognizing a fulfilled promise offers only a general praise response.
It calls people to believe in the messenger for their good while grounding all creation in God.
It explicitly joins repentance, faith, and righteous action with the hope of being among the successful.
The call to enter fully into submission is broadly compatible with obedience but lacks the focus's specific elements.
God's doing what He wills does not explain the human commands or success in the focus.
It supplies the bodily purification required when rising for prayer, a practical preparation for worship.
The question about forbidding what God made lawful does not materially clarify the focus.
The sorcerers' being cast down in prostration provides a vivid responsive instance of surrender.
It identifies God as Lord of the present audience and their forefathers, grounding exclusive devotion.
It portrays believers who, when reminded of God's signs, fall prostrate, praise their Lord, and reject arrogance.
It associates beautiful reward with those who do good, adding an outcome for beneficent conduct.
Its dream of celestial bodies prostrating to Joseph is a different narrative use of prostration.
It describes servants of the Merciful through humble walking and peaceful speech, giving social shape to good conduct.
It frames recompense as a return for what disbelievers used to do, reinforcing action's consequences.
The nearby creation-and-resurrection argument does not directly develop worship, good action, or success.
The angels' prostration before Adam is a distinct commanded scene and is less direct than earlier worship parallels.
It joins establishing prayer, giving alms, and sending forward every good deed for God.
It joins surrendering oneself to God with doing good and its promised reward.
It gives a broad account of righteousness in belief, worship, generosity, and steadfast ethical action.
It explicitly joins faith, righteous deeds, prayer, and almsgiving with God's reward.
It portrays believers who command good, forbid wrong, and hasten to good deeds.
It defines God-conscious good conduct through generosity, restraint of anger, and forgiveness.
It promises that no good work of a believing man or woman is lost to God.
It directly commands establishing prayer and giving alms after calling believers to restraint and God-consciousness.
It names charity, recognized good, and reconciliation as beneficial deeds done seeking God's approval.
It joins faith and righteous deeds with enduring entry into gardens.
It makes righteous deeds joined to faith the basis for entering the Garden without injustice.
It includes prayer, almsgiving, faith in the messengers, and generous lending among covenantal obligations.
It identifies the believing community through prayer, almsgiving, and bowing.
It repeatedly joins faith, God-consciousness, and doing good while affirming that God loves those who do good.
It commands establishment of prayer and God-consciousness before the final gathering to Him.
It gathers prayer, sacrifice, life, and death under exclusive devotion to God.
It depicts those near God as neither too proud to worship Him nor unwilling to prostrate.
It describes believers whose faith responds to God's mention and whose reliance is on their Lord.
It completes that believer profile with establishing prayer and spending from provision.
It joins mutual moral responsibility, prayer, almsgiving, and obedience among believing women and men.
It directs establishment of prayer and states that good deeds remove evil deeds.
It combines patience, prayer, charitable spending, and repelling evil with good.
It commands believing servants to establish prayer and spend before the final Day.
It commands justice, excellence, and giving to relatives while forbidding indecency and wrongdoing.
It promises a good life and a better reward to every believer who does righteous deeds.
It joins desire for the Hereafter, fitting effort, and faith as the basis for accepted striving.
It commands the establishment of prayer across its appointed times.
It affirms that God does not let the reward of those who believe and do good be lost.
It joins hope of meeting God with righteous action and exclusive worship of the Lord.
It joins prayer and almsgiving among the abiding commands given to Jesus.
It describes Ishmael as commanding his people to prayer and almsgiving.
It directly commands worship of God and establishment of prayer for His remembrance.
It commands steadfastly maintaining prayer within one's household and links provision to God-consciousness.
It joins doing good, establishing prayer, giving alms, and devoted worship in one description of guided leaders.
It describes those whose hearts respond to God's mention, who persevere, establish prayer, and spend from provision.
It clarifies that sacrificial rites reach God through God-consciousness rather than their material offerings.
It joins established prayer, almsgiving, enjoining right, and forbidding wrong as the conduct of the empowered.
It opens the believers' profile by directly declaring their success.
It identifies humble attentiveness in prayer as an initial trait of the successful believers.
It identifies careful preservation of prayers as part of the same successful believer profile.
It portrays people whom trade does not divert from God's remembrance, prayer, or almsgiving.
It directly commands prayer, almsgiving, and obedience to the messenger in expectation of mercy.
It joins repentance, faith, and righteous action, with God transforming evil deeds into good ones.
It commands prayer and presents it as restraining indecency and wrongdoing.
It calls for turning to God, being God-conscious, and establishing prayer without associating others with Him.
It joins prayer, enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and patient endurance in a father's counsel.
It gathers devotion, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity, fasting, chastity, and remembrance among faithful qualities.
It joins reverent fear of God, prayer, and self-purification.
It makes worship of God alone the condition for deeds not being nullified.
It contrasts evil's measured recompense with the unbounded provision of believing righteous actors.
It describes believers who answer their Lord, establish prayer, deliberate together, and spend from provision.
It directly states that God is Lord and commands worship of Him as the straight path.
It commands obedience to God and the messenger and warns against rendering deeds void.
It states worship of God as the purpose for which jinn and humankind were created.
It renews the commands to establish prayer, give alms, and obey God and the messenger.
It commands God-consciousness and self-examination of what each person has sent ahead.
It commands believers to hasten to God's remembrance when called to the congregational prayer.
It distinguishes those devoted to prayer within the wider description of human impatience.
It joins prayer, almsgiving, and lending God a good loan in a concluding practical command.
It joins remembering the name of one's Lord with prayer immediately after the declaration of success.
It directly declares successful the one who purifies the self.
It joins sincere worship, upright devotion, prayer, and almsgiving in a concise religious command.
It joins faith, righteous deeds, truth, and patient perseverance as the exception from loss.
